title: Bandwidth, Peak Rates & PoE
summary: What faster Wi-Fi asks of the switches, cabling and power behind every access point.

opener.promise: Switches, cabling and power that let Wi-Fi 7 deliver
opener.problem: New access points on old switch ports and power budgets cannot reach their potential.

beats.heading: New access points, old wiring closets

caption.headline: New access points, old wiring closets
caption.takeaway: A Wi-Fi 7 project is also a wired-network project: budget switches, power and cabling together.

beats.body:
A hospital plans a Wi-Fi 7 refresh for a new wing. The wireless side looks fast — but each [[access-point|access point]] still plugs into a switch port, through a cable, drawing its power from that switch.

If the switch ports are 1 Gb/s {{gigabit-1}} and the power budget was sized for older access points, the new radios cannot deliver what they promise.
beats.bottomLine: A Wi-Fi 7 project is also a wired-network project; budget for switches, power and cabling at the same time.
beats.sceneDescription: The access point is drawn as a sprinkler head on the ceiling, fed from the wiring closet by one pipe that carries both data and power. On an old 1 Gb/s port {{gigabit-1}} the pipe is thin and the spray from two nozzles is weak. The power gauge on the closet sits below the red line showing what the access point needs, so two nozzles, standing for radios, stay dry.

callout.title: Old closets hold back new radios
points: Each access point gets data and power through one switch port
An old 1 Gb/s port is a thin pipe{{gigabit-1}}
Too little power, and some radios switch off

beats.heading: Peak rates by generation

caption.headline: Peak rates are a ceiling, not a forecast
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 7’s theoretical peak is 46.1 Gbps{{wifi7-peak-phy}}; real devices and networks achieve far less.
caption.technical: Assumes 16 [[spatial-stream|spatial streams]]{{eht-max-nss}}; the [[phy-rate|PHY rate]] is raw signalling, and MAC throughput is lower{{be-mac-throughput-goal}}.

beats.body:
Each generation raised the theoretical [[phy-rate|PHY rate]] — the raw over-the-air signalling speed. Wi-Fi 4 tops out at 600 Mbps {{wifi4-peak-phy}}, Wi-Fi 5 at 6.93 Gbps {{wifi5-peak-phy}}, Wi-Fi 6 at 9.61 Gbps {{wifi6-peak-phy}} and Wi-Fi 7 at 46.1 Gbps {{wifi7-peak-phy}}.

These are theoretical maximums with every option at its limit, including 16 [[spatial-stream|spatial streams]] for Wi-Fi 7 {{eht-max-nss}}. A device with fewer streams has a proportionally lower peak, and usable throughput is lower still {{be-mac-throughput-goal}}.
beats.bottomLine: Treat peak rates as a ceiling, not a forecast: the meaningful number is the throughput your devices and environment actually achieve.
beats.sceneDescription: A close view of the sprinkler head. A large wireframe spray shows its rated maximum, labelled with Wi-Fi 7’s theoretical peak rate {{wifi7-peak-phy}}, and the earlier generation’s rated maximum is noted beneath. The solid spray inside it, much smaller, is what real devices actually get.

questions.q: Why show a theoretical peak that no device reaches?
questions.a: It is the standard’s ceiling with 16 spatial streams{{eht-max-nss}}, useful only to compare generations. Real throughput depends on device streams, channel width and sharing; ask vendors for tested throughput instead.

callout.title: The number on the box
points: That assumes 16 spatial streams, more than devices have{{eht-max-nss}}
Ask vendors for tested throughput instead

beats.heading: Faster uplinks and more power per port

caption.headline: Faster [[uplink|uplinks]] and more power per port
caption.takeaway: [[multigig|Multi-gigabit]] uplinks{{multigig-2-5-5}} and higher [[poe|PoE]] classes, up to 90 W{{poe-type4-pse}}, become planning items.
caption.technical: Power at the device is lower after cable loss: 71.3 W for Type 4{{poe-type4-pd}}.

beats.body:
Even below its PHY rate, a Wi-Fi 7 access point can move more traffic than a 1 Gb/s link carries: 802.11be targets at least 30 Gb/s at the [[mac-layer|MAC layer]] {{be-mac-throughput-goal}}. [[multigig|Multi-gigabit Ethernet]] — 2.5 and 5 Gb/s {{multigig-2-5-5}} or 10 Gb/s {{multigig-10}} — gives the [[uplink]] headroom over existing twisted-pair cabling.

[[poe|Power over Ethernet]] comes in classes: 15.4 W {{poe-type1-pse}}, 30 W {{poe-type2-pse}}, 60 W {{poe-type3-pse}} and 90 W {{poe-type4-pse}} at the switch port.
beats.bottomLine: Plan switch ports and power budgets from each access point model's specifications, not from the previous generation's.
beats.deepDive: Power figures are at the power-sourcing equipment (switch port). After cable losses, the powered device receives about 12.95 W {{poe-type1-pd}}, 25.5 W {{poe-type2-pd}}, 51 W {{poe-type3-pd}} or 71.3 W {{poe-type4-pd}}. Types 1–2 come from 802.3af/at and Types 3–4 from 802.3bt, all consolidated in IEEE 802.3-2022 {{poe-type3-pse}}. Multi-gigabit PHYs are 2.5GBASE-T and 5GBASE-T {{multigig-2-5-5}} and 10GBASE-T {{multigig-10}}.
beats.sceneDescription: The pipe widens into a multi-gigabit port, labelled with its speeds {{multigig-2-5-5}} {{multigig-10}}, and water flows freely along it. The power gauge rises above the red line, with the PoE classes marked beside it from 15.4 W {{poe-type1-pse}} to 90 W {{poe-type4-pse}}. All four nozzles spray at full strength.

questions.q: Do we need to recable for Wi-Fi 7?
questions.a: Often not. 2.5GBASE-T and 5GBASE-T run multi-gigabit speeds over existing twisted-pair cabling{{multigig-2-5-5}}; verify cable runs during the survey, and plan 10 Gb/s{{multigig-10}} only where it is needed.

questions.q: How much PoE does a Wi-Fi 7 access point need?
questions.a: It varies by model and enabled features. Classes range from 15.4 W{{poe-type1-pse}} to 90 W{{poe-type4-pse}} at the switch port; check each model’s documented class, and whether features switch off at lower power.

callout.title: A wider pipe and more power
points: [[multigig|Multi-gigabit]] ports run 2.5 or 5 Gb/s on existing cable{{multigig-2-5-5}}
Higher [[poe|PoE]] classes deliver up to 90 W per port{{poe-type4-pse}}
Check each model’s documented power class

beats.heading: What changes in the wired network

caption.headline: What changes in the wired network
caption.takeaway: 1 Gb/s ports{{gigabit-1}} can cap new access points; expect to upgrade access-layer switches alongside.
caption.technical: Peak rate is streams × subcarriers × bits × coding rate ÷ symbol time{{wifi7-peak-phy}}.

beats.body:
Access points from the Wi-Fi 5 era commonly ran on 1 Gb/s ports {{gigabit-1}}. With Wi-Fi 7's higher capacity, multi-gigabit uplinks {{multigig-2-5-5}} and higher PoE classes {{poe-type3-pse}} become planning considerations for each access point model.

Check each model's documented power class and uplink speed, and size switch power budgets for every port on the floor.
beats.bottomLine: Expect to refresh or upgrade access-layer switches alongside Wi-Fi 7; leaving old switches in place can cap the benefit of new access points.
beats.deepDive: Peak PHY rates are derived from IEEE parameters: streams × data [[subcarrier|subcarriers]] × bits per subcarrier × coding rate ÷ symbol time {{wifi7-peak-phy}}. Usable MAC throughput is lower {{be-mac-throughput-goal}}, and an access point's uplink carries the sum of its radios' traffic. Exact power draw depends on the radios and features enabled; access points may disable features at lower PoE classes, so confirm behaviour per model.
beats.sceneDescription: Two closets side by side. On the left, the earlier generation’s access point has two nozzles and runs fully on a thin 1 Gb/s pipe {{gigabit-1}}, because it needed less. On the right, the Wi-Fi 7 access point has four nozzles on a wide multi-gigabit pipe with a fuller power gauge.

callout.title: What changes in the closet
points: Older access points ran fine on 1 Gb/s ports{{gigabit-1}}
Wi-Fi 7 needs multi-gigabit ports{{multigig-2-5-5}} and more power{{poe-type3-pse}}
Expect to upgrade access-layer switches alongside

beats.heading: Planning closets, budgets and timelines

caption.headline: Plan closets, budgets and timelines early
caption.takeaway: Put switching, PoE budgets and cabling checks in the business case from the start.

beats.body:
For a hospital floor, the wired side often decides the schedule and the budget: switch replacements, power supplies, cabling checks and maintenance windows in clinical areas.

Planning these early avoids installing new access points that are throttled by old switch ports or unable to power all of their features.
beats.bottomLine: Include switching, PoE budget and cabling verification in the Wi-Fi 7 business case and project timeline from the start.
beats.sceneDescription: An upgraded wiring closet feeds three sprinkler heads across the floor through wide pipes, with the power gauge above the line, and every nozzle sprays at full strength.

callout.title: What to put in the plan
points: Switch upgrades and multi-gigabit ports for every access point
A PoE power budget for every port on the floor
Cabling checks and clinical-area maintenance windows
